title: PhD Research: Hydrogen and Methane Aircraft Safety
text:
Liquid hydrogen (H\(_2\)) and methane (CH\(_4\)) are leading candidates for decarbonizing long-haul aviation. However, these fuels differ substantially from Jet A in their leak and ignition behavior, requiring systemic safety considerations from the earliest design phases.
This research connects three domains: certification frameworks, hazard physics, and aircraft performance. I couple leak-consequence solvers (such as HyRAM+) with multidisciplinary design optimization (MDO) to quantify how passive leak-mitigation requirements affect transport efficiency across fuels and tank architectures.








TipHeadline results




Safety has a measurable cost, and it depends on how much leakage you design to tolerate. For a 7500 nmi, 400-passenger commercial transport mission (Boeing 777-300ER-class), designing for a 10 mg/s passive-threshold leak rate (PTLR) raises passenger-specific transport energy by roughly 2-5%. At 20 mg/s, the increase is roughly 3-11%.
Spatial separation drives the penalty, not ventilation. Keeping hot jets due to fuel-leak-supplied flames away from structure grows the aircraft, and is especially impactful if driving the wing geometry. Ventilation drag to mitigate leaked fuel buildup and subsequent explosion risk is a minor contributor.
Methane is penalized more than hydrogen at the same leak rate because its flames require larger offsets.









Figure 1: Model-optimized aircraft with a 20 mg/s PTLR.



Full results are in Key Results; the framework and models behind them are in Methods.



Jet A forms slowly evaporating pools with small ignitable regions. Leaked H\(_2\) and CH\(_4\) behave very differently: they vaporize quickly, mix readily with air, form larger ignitable regions, and ignite at much lower energies. As a result, tanks should stay at positive pressure with a gaseous-fuel ullage, which prevents ignitable boil-off/air mixtures from forming inside them.






Figure 2: Qualitative comparison of leak and fire safety behavior for Jet A versus H\(_2\) and CH\(_4\).



Ground-based hydrogen systems offer a baseline set of leak-mitigation strategies. However, there is no established way to apply them to aircraft or to relate them to certification requirements. This work aims to fill that gap.

title: PhD Research: Hydrogen and Methane Aircraft Safety
text:
Key Contributions

Designated Leak Zone (DLZ) framework. A formal classification of leak zones for H\(_2\)- and CH\(_4\)-fueled aircraft, modeled on the 14 CFR § 25.1181 fire zones used for Jet A, to handle the unique vapor and ignition risks of alternative fuels.
Physics-based consequence modeling. Leak-consequence models that map the ventilation flow rates and spatial separations needed to passively mitigate jet fires, explosions, and cryogenic damage.
MDO integration. An aircraft design procedure that optimizes vehicle configuration under leak-safety constraints. It evaluates transport energy as a function of fuel, tank layout, and the maximum leak rate mitigated passively, termed the passive-threshold leak rate (PTLR).
Performance impact quantification. Flame-driven spatial separation (especially for wing geometries) dominates system-level penalties over ventilation requirements. At equal leak rates, CH\(_4\) incurs larger penalties because of its larger spatial offsets.

title: PhD Research: Hydrogen and Methane Aircraft Safety
text:
Methods
The sections below describe the leak-safety framework, the consequence models, and the MDO setup behind the results above.

Designated Leak Zones and the Proposed Leak Safety Framework
The framework rests on two constructs: designated leak zones (DLZs) and passive-threshold leak rates (PTLRs).
The hazard zone definitions are informed by FAR 25.863 (flammable fluid fire protection) and FAR 25.1181 (designated fire zones). Zones are defined by their proximity to fuel and to heat or ignition sources:

Fuel zone: the internal volume of fuel-containing components, such as tanks and pipes, where liquid, supercritical, or gaseous fuel is present during normal operation.
Designated leak zone (DLZ): any region where leaked fuel could enter or accumulate. This includes compartments containing fuel-system components and regions that fuel lines or fittings pass through, but excludes regions continuously open to the external atmosphere.
Designated fire zone: a region associated with equipment identified under FAR 25.1181, such as engine and auxiliary power unit compartments, where flammable fluids and high-temperature ignition sources may coexist. These zones must meet the applicable designated fire zone requirements.
Occupied areas: areas where occupants and cargo are present during normal operations. They may contain ignition sources associated with people, equipment, or cargo. Fuel shall not be present in occupied areas during normal operations or single-failure scenarios.







Figure 7: Hazard zone classification for hydrogen and methane aircraft, shown for an illustrative forward-aft fuel tank configuration. Fuel zones and occupied areas are pressurized relative to the designated leak zone, which is maintained at lower pressure than the adjacent protected zones or is unpressurized.









Figure 8: Hazard zones for the ventral fuel tank configuration.



Two requirements follow from these definitions:

Adjacency. A single failure may not introduce flammable fluids into occupied areas. Occupied areas therefore cannot be adjacent to designated fire zones or fuel zones; a DLZ must sit between them as a leak-mitigation buffer.
Pressurization. This localizes single-failure leak consequences to the DLZ. Fuel zones are kept at positive pressure relative to the DLZ, so a loss of containment pushes fuel outward into the DLZ. Occupied areas are also kept at positive pressure relative to the DLZ, which biases leaked fuel away from the cabin. Managing leaks within the DLZ is then the primary means of preventing personnel exposure.







Figure 9: Leak consequences are localized and managed within DLZs.





Passive-Threshold Leak Rate (PTLR)
Leak consequences, and the design needed to mitigate them, depend on leak rate. Passive mitigation is always available, but its design requirements scale with the leak rate it must accommodate, so a characteristic leak rate must be chosen. That rate, expressed as a fuel mass flow rate, is the passive-threshold leak rate (PTLR).
An aircraft’s PTLR is the maximum leak rate for which it is passively safe, meaning safe without leak detection or response.






Figure 10: The passive-threshold leak rate (PTLR) is the maximum leak rate for which a DLZ is passively safe.



Choosing the PTLR is a balance against the acceptable-risk criteria of FAR 25.1309:






Figure 11: FAR 25.1309 acceptable risk for all systems.









Figure 12: If the PTLR is underspecified, the requirements of FAR 25.1309 are not met.









Figure 13: If the PTLR is overspecified, the requirements of FAR 25.1309 are met, but unnecessary performance penalties are incurred.









Figure 14: The performance-optimal PTLR: aircraft-level performance penalties are minimized while still meeting the requirements of FAR 25.1309.





Leak Consequence Modeling
Each DLZ is represented by a simplified duct-like segment, and parametric models estimate the consequences of a leak within it.






Figure 15: Simplified leak zone segment used for parametric hazard analysis. Fuel is released from a local leak source into a duct-like segment that may be ventilated along its length.



Leak source. Models disagree substantially for cryogenic leaks near saturation, with mass-flux differences up to about 8\(\times\).






Figure 16: Comparison of orifice-flow model predictions for cryogenic hydrogen and methane leaks from a 145 kPa upstream state to 30 kPa ambient pressure. Results are shown versus upstream temperature, with the hydrogen and methane temperature axes aligned relative to each fuel’s boiling point at 145 kPa. For saturated-liquid and two-phase upstream conditions, the predicted leak-exit density, speed, and mass flux vary substantially across models, with mass-flux differences up to approximately 8\(\times\). For gaseous upstream conditions sufficiently above the boiling point, the HyRAM and classical gas choked-flow predictions agree closely.



Explosion mitigation. Ventilation limits the accumulated fuel mass, and thereby the overpressure from combustion.






Figure 17: Estimated overpressure in a 30 m\(^3\) reference leak zone as a function of leak rate and ventilation speed. Contours show the ratio of pressure increase to ambient pressure from combustion of accumulated fuel. Increasing ventilation reduces the accumulated fuel mass and lowers the overpressure. Model by Bauwens and Dorofeev.









Figure 18: Ventilation speed required to meet explosion-mitigation criteria as a function of leak rate for the 1 m\(^2\), 30 m long reference leak zone. Criteria include keeping the bulk fuel-air concentration below 25% of the lower flammability limit (LFL) and limiting overpressure to selected target values.



Jet fire and heating. Spatial separation and ventilation determine how hot nearby structure gets.






Figure 19: Model used for component-specific heating analysis, where heat equation is solved using py-pde and accounting for convective heat transfer from flame to component, convective cooling of ventilation air, and radiation to and from the component.









Figure 20: Steady-state maximum temperature of a 0.125-inch Al-7075-T6 plate as a function of spatial separation (horizontal axis) and ventilation speed (vertical axis) for hydrogen (left) and methane (right) at leak rates of 100 mg/s (top) and 1000 mg/s (bottom). Background conditions are assumed for an altitude of 8000 m.









Figure 21: Metrics evaluated for spatial separation requirements that protect nearby structures from jet-flame thermal hazard.









Figure 22: Visible flame length, unobstructed 100 °C distance, and component-specific 100 °C distance as a function of leak mass flow rate for cryogenic liquid hydrogen and methane. Unobstructed 100 °C distances provide a conservative upper bound for PTLRs greater than $$10-30 mg/s.



Summary. Together, these parametric models feed the aircraft-level optimization.






Figure 23: Summary of parametric consequence models and outputs.





MDO Implementation
The consequence models enter the aircraft design optimization as constraints, for both tank layouts.






Figure 24: Forward-aft fuel tank configuration and MDO implementation.









Figure 25: Ventral fuel tank configuration and MDO implementation.

title: Firefly: Deployable-Tail Micro-UAV
text:
As part of my S.M. research at the MIT International Center for Air Transportation, I led the design and development of the stability and control system for Firefly—a deployable micro-UAV powered by a slow-burning solid rocket motor.
The challenge involved engineering a reliable tail deployment mechanism that could transition seamlessly from a compact stowed configuration to a stable flying wing/tail architecture under changing vehicle static margin as the solid-rocket motor burned.






Figure 1: Firefly Concept of Operations.

title: Firefly: Deployable-Tail Micro-UAV
text:
As part of my S.M. research at the MIT International Center for Air Transportation, I led the design and development of the stability and control system for Firefly—a deployable micro-UAV powered by a slow-burning solid rocket motor.
The challenge involved engineering a reliable tail deployment mechanism that could transition seamlessly from a compact stowed configuration to a stable flying wing/tail architecture under changing vehicle static margin as the solid-rocket motor burned.






Figure 1: Firefly Concept of Operations.

title: Firefly: Deployable-Tail Micro-UAV
text:
Key Contributions & Technical Highlights

Folding-Tail Mechanism: Designed a pull-spring-actuated folding tail utilizing an oblique hinge that serves as both the physical deployment axis and the aerodynamic actuation axis.
Rapid Prototyping: Iterated rapidly through multiple 3D-printable vehicle iterations to test hinge mechanics, deployment reliability, and structural integrity.
Wind-Tunnel Testing: Built a custom pitch-balance test setup to experimentally evaluate longitudinal stability and controllability across various angles of attack.
Flight Testing: Conducted unpowered drop tests deployed from a quadcopter to collect stability and controllability data under glide conditions.
Validation: Correlated experimental wind-tunnel and drop-test data against analytical predictions generated via AVL (Athena Vortex Lattice).

title: Desktop Lathe: MIT Course 2.720 Team Project
text: This team hardware prototyping project, as part of MIT course 2.720, focused on the design, fabrication, and requirements verification of a custom desktop lathe. Precision mechanical design and rapid prototyping methods were employed to build a functional, benchtop-scale machining tool capable of turning stainless steel during the one semester long course.

title: Desktop Lathe: MIT Course 2.720 Team Project
text: This team hardware prototyping project, as part of MIT course 2.720, focused on the design, fabrication, and requirements verification of a custom desktop lathe. Precision mechanical design and rapid prototyping methods were employed to build a functional, benchtop-scale machining tool capable of turning stainless steel during the one semester long course.

title: Desktop Lathe: MIT Course 2.720 Team Project
text:
Key Contributions & Technical Highlights

Precision Manufacturing: Designed and machined aluminum and stainless steel spindle components and integrated the motor-to-spindle power transmission system.
Part & System Functional Requirements Verification: Post-manufacturing verification, using tools including a Coordinate Measuring Machine (CMM), was conducted to verify parts met specified tolerances and stiffness requirements.

Iterative Pulley Geometry Prototyping: Designed and tested multiple crowned pulley geometries using 3D-printing to rapidly evaluate belt tracking and stability before committing to final fabrication geometry.
Functional Validation: Performed cut testing, successfully demonstrating the lathe’s capability to cleanly turn stainless steel stock.

title: Rocketry: MIT Rocket Team and Tripoli Certification Flights
text: During my undergraduate studes, my involvement with the MIT Rocket Team included leadership roles as President and Propulsion Lead. The team focused on high-altitude solid-motor rocket flights utilizing in-house formulated and mixed solid rocket propellant alongside fully custom motors. In addition to team projects, I designed and flew personal rockets for Tripoli Rocketry Association certification, culminating in an L3 certification (the highest level) achieved with a scratch-built rocket.
